title: The structure of small-scale and large-scale spatial skills and their relations with mathematics performance
abstract: Abstract Spatial skills are consistently associated with mathematics performance, yet the role of scale is rarely considered. There remains an open question about how small-scale versus large-scale spatial skills relate to distinct domains of mathematics. In the present study, the structure of spatial skills and their relation to mathematics performance was examined using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). A total of 248 undergraduate students residing in a major urban center ( M = 20 years, 8 months, 63.7% female) completed an online battery of assessments measuring cognitive skills (perspective taking, mental rotation, navigation, and fluid reasoning) and mathematics abilities (geometry and number). Factor analysis revealed a three-factor structure of cognitive skills: (1) small-scale spatial skills (combining perspective taking and mental rotation), (2) large-scale navigation skills, and (3) fluid reasoning. The SEM results showed a significant path from small-scale spatial skills to mathematics performance, with this relation partially mediated by fluid reasoning. Although navigation was correlated with small-scale spatial skills, it was not related to mathematics outcomes in the SEM. Further multivariate regression analyses indicated that fluid reasoning was significantly associated with both number and geometry performance, while perspective taking accounted for unique variance in number task performance. These findings underscore the crucial role of perspective taking within the domain of small-scale spatial skills and highlight the nuanced, domain-specific contributions of distinct spatial and cognitive skills to mathematical thinking.
